A wafer map records each chip's test result (good or failure type) by position on the wafer. The packaging stage uses this map to exclude bad chips. Patterns such as failures clustered at the edge or center also help trace which process has a problem.

Why the others are wrong
· Option 1: Circuit patterns are made in lithography. The wafer map is for recording test results.
· Option 2: Wafer specs are set during wafer manufacturing and have nothing to do with the wafer map.
· Option 4: Printing brand or lot information is the marking process, not the purpose of a wafer map.

💡 Key point: Wafer map = record of failure locations → exclusion (packaging) + root-cause tracing (yield).

question: What is repair at the EDS stage for memory chips?
options: Re-exposing the circuit patterns of bad chips to fix them
Grinding the wafer to physically remove bad chips
Opening the package and re-bonding broken wires
Replacing failing cells with built-in spare (redundancy) cells to save the chip
explanation:
Answer explanation
Memory chips have enormous numbers of cells, so some cells easily fail. Spare cells (redundancy) are built in ahead of time, and when EDS finds failing cells, they're swapped for spares — for example by blowing fuses — so the whole chip is saved as good. This raises yield.

Why the others are wrong
· Option 1: Circuit patterns that are already made can't be fixed by re-exposure.
· Option 2: Bad chips aren't ground away; they're recorded on the wafer map and excluded at packaging.
· Option 3: Packages aren't opened to fix wires. Repair happens at the wafer stage, before packaging.

💡 Key point: Repair = failing cells → swapped for spare cells → yield goes up.

question: Which is NOT a test done at the EDS stage?
options: DC parametric tests that measure terminal voltage and current to find shorts or opens
Package delamination inspection to check whether the molding resin has separated from the substrate
Function tests that check whether the chip works as designed
Speed (AC) tests that check whether it works correctly at the specified speed
explanation:
Answer explanation
EDS checks chips' electrical characteristics at the wafer stage, before packaging, so it includes DC, function and speed tests. Molding resin is the material that encases chips during packaging, so delamination inspection belongs to post-packaging reliability and visual inspection.

Why the others are wrong
· Option 1: DC parametric testing is a classic EDS item that quickly screens out fatal failures such as shorts and opens.
· Option 3: Function testing is done in EDS, applying patterns to check that the chip behaves as designed.
· Option 4: Speed testing at the specified speed is also an EDS test item.

💡 Key point: EDS is electrical testing at the wafer stage. Package-related inspection is back-end.

question: Which correctly describes a structural feature of NAND flash memory?
options: Each cell connects directly and separately to the bit line in parallel
Each cell has a capacitor, so periodic refresh is needed
Several cells are connected in series in a string, so cell area is small and density is high
Each cell contains six transistors, so it's large
explanation:
Answer explanation
NAND links cells in series into a single line (string). Since each cell doesn't need its own bit-line contact, cell area shrinks, making it suited to high-capacity storage. In exchange, reading any single cell at random is slower than in NOR.

Why the others are wrong
· Option 1: Cells connected to the bit line in parallel is NOR flash's structure, which gives fast random access but larger cells.
· Option 2: A capacitor per cell with refresh is DRAM. NAND is non-volatile and needs no refresh.
· Option 4: Six transistors per cell is SRAM.

💡 Key point: NAND = series strings (high density); NOR = parallel (fast random reads).

question: What is the most appropriate description of DRAM's role in a computer?
options: Permanently storing the operating system and programs even after power is off
Serving as main memory that temporarily holds programs and data the CPU is about to use
Serving as the registers and L1 cache that hold values being computed inside the CPU
Keeping boot settings that persist when power is off
explanation:
Answer explanation
DRAM is main memory that holds running programs and data so the CPU can fetch them right away. It's high-capacity and inexpensive, but volatile, so its contents disappear when power is off.

Why the others are wrong
· Option 1: Permanent storage is the job of storage devices such as SSDs (NAND flash) or HDDs. DRAM loses data when power is off.
· Option 3: Registers and L1 cache are faster memory inside the CPU, mainly built from SRAM.
· Option 4: Information that must survive power-off, like boot settings, goes in non-volatile memory such as flash or ROM.

💡 Key point: DRAM = main memory (temporary, fast, high-capacity); SSD = permanent storage.

question: Which correctly describes the structure and role of a TSV (through-silicon via)?
options: A mask used to engrave circuit patterns on the chip surface
Resin that encases the chip to protect it from external impact
A polishing process that grinds down height differences on the wafer surface
A passage drilled vertically through silicon and filled with copper to directly connect chips above and below
explanation:
Answer explanation
A TSV is a via drilled vertically through a silicon chip or wafer, lined with insulator and diffusion barrier, then filled with a conductor such as copper. Chips are stacked vertically and exchange signals and power through these passages. It's a core technology for stacked memory such as HBM.

Why the others are wrong
· Option 1: Engraving circuit patterns is done with photomasks and exposure.
· Option 2: Encasing and protecting the chip is molding resin. A TSV is an electrical connection path.
· Option 3: Polishing the wafer flat is CMP.

💡 Key point: TSV = a vertical connection path made by filling a through-silicon via with conductor.

question: Which correctly describes the difference between SiP (system in package) and SoC (system on chip)?
options: SiP integrates every function on one die, while SoC puts several chips in one package
SiP ships wafers as is, without packaging
SiP puts several chips in one package, while SoC integrates functions on one die
SiP and SoC are just different names for the same concept
explanation:
Answer explanation
An SoC integrates functions such as the CPU, GPU and memory controller on a single die. A SiP places several separately made chips and passive components in one package so they work together as a system. Its advantages are mixing chips from different processes (logic, memory, RF, etc.) and shorter development time.

Why the others are wrong
· Option 1: Gathering functions on one die is SoC, not SiP. The descriptions are swapped.
· Option 2: SiP is also a packaged product; it isn't sold as wafers.
· Option 4: They're implemented differently: SiP integrates at the package level, SoC at the die level.

💡 Key point: SoC = integrated on one die; SiP = several chips integrated in one package.

question: Which is an advantage of using graphene as a transistor channel?
options: Its large band gap makes off-state leakage very small
Its low thermal conductivity traps heat well
Its electron mobility is very high
Its low production cost makes it the best for mass production
explanation:
Answer explanation
Graphene is a single-atom-thick sheet of carbon with very high electron mobility and high thermal conductivity, which favors high-speed devices. But its band gap is nearly zero, so turning a transistor fully off is hard — its biggest challenge.

Why the others are wrong
· Option 1: Graphene's band gap is nearly zero, so current flows easily even when off. That's the main reason it's hard to use in transistors.
· Option 2: Graphene has very high thermal conductivity. Saying it's low is wrong.
· Option 4: Making high-quality graphene uniformly over large areas is still hard, so mass production isn't its main strength.

💡 Key point: Graphene = high mobility and thermal conductivity; drawback: no band gap (hard to turn off).

question: What happens when a voltage at or above the threshold voltage (Vth) is applied to the gate of an n-type MOSFET?
options: The path between source and drain is blocked and no current flows at all
The gate oxide becomes a conductor and a large gate current flows
An electron channel (inversion layer) forms under the gate, and current flows between source and drain
Holes in the substrate rise into the conduction band and the device heats up
explanation:
Answer explanation
An n-type MOSFET's substrate is P-type. With a positive gate voltage at or above threshold, electrons gather at the surface under the gate to form an inversion layer (channel), connecting source and drain so current flows. Below threshold, there's no channel and the device is off.

Why the others are wrong
· Option 1: At or above threshold, a channel forms and the device turns on. Source and drain are disconnected below threshold, in the off state.
· Option 2: The oxide stays an insulator. If it became a conductor, the device would be broken.
· Option 4: What happens above threshold isn't hole movement but the formation of an electron inversion layer at the surface.

💡 Key point: Vgs ≥ Vth → inversion layer (channel) forms → ON.

question: What advantage does hybrid bonding have over micro-bump bonding?
options: The bonding surfaces need almost no flatness or cleanliness, so the process is easy
It doesn't use copper, so connection resistance actually increases
The gap between chips widens, greatly improving heat dissipation
Copper pads bond directly without solder bumps, allowing a much finer bond pitch
explanation:
Answer explanation
Hybrid bonding first joins the insulating films (mainly SiO₂) on the chip surfaces, then bonds the copper pads within them directly by annealing. With no solder bumps, the bond pitch can shrink to the micrometer scale, the number of connections rises sharply, and resistance and spacing shrink. In exchange, surfaces must be extremely flat and clean, so CMP and cleanliness control are demanding.

Why the others are wrong
· Option 1: It's the opposite: it's very sensitive to surface flatness and particle contamination, so CMP and cleanliness are the core challenges.
· Option 2: Hybrid bonding joins copper pads directly, so saying it doesn't use copper is wrong.
· Option 3: With no bumps, the gap between chips actually shrinks. Heat dissipation isn't its key advantage.

💡 Key point: Hybrid bonding = direct Cu–Cu plus dielectric bonding, no bumps → fine pitch, many connections. Challenges: flatness and cleanliness.

question: What is the core technology for stacking several DRAM dies vertically and connecting them in HBM?
options: Connecting edge pads with wire bonding alone
Connecting them directly with TSVs and micro bumps (or hybrid bonding)
Filling the space between dies with molding resin to connect them
Attaching the dies side by side on a lead frame
explanation:
Answer explanation
HBM stacks DRAM dies in layers, runs TSVs through each die, and connects them above and below directly with micro bumps. Hybrid bonding is also being considered for next-generation products with taller stacks. This makes connections short and numerous, delivering wide bandwidth.

Why the others are wrong
· Option 1: Wire bonding alone can't connect many signals over short distances in a multi-layer stack, so it doesn't suit HBM.
· Option 3: Molding resin encases and protects chips; it doesn't make electrical connections between dies.
· Option 4: Placing dies side by side on a lead frame isn't stacking and can't reach HBM's bandwidth.

💡 Key point: HBM = stacked DRAM + TSVs + micro bumps (or hybrid bonding).

question: What is HBM's biggest advantage over regular DRAM modules (DDR)?
options: Stored data stays intact even when power is off
Its process is simple, so it's much cheaper than regular DRAM
A single die handles all the capacity, so no stacking is needed
TSV stacking and a wide I/O interface give it much higher memory bandwidth
explanation:
Answer explanation
HBM stacks DRAM dies, connects them with TSVs to create a wide I/O of 1024 bits or more per stack, and sits close to the processor with short connections. The wide interface moves a lot of data at once, so it's used in high-bandwidth systems such as AI accelerators. In exchange, stacking and packaging are complex, so it's expensive.

Why the others are wrong
· Option 1: HBM is still DRAM, so it's volatile; data disappears when power is off.
· Option 2: HBM needs TSVs and stacked packaging, so the process is complex and the price high.
· Option 3: HBM stacks multiple dies to increase capacity and bandwidth.

💡 Key point: HBM = stacking + TSVs + wide I/O → bandwidth ↑ (but complex and costly).

question: Which lists the 8 major chipmaking processes in the correct order?
options: Wafer manufacturing → photo → oxidation → etch → deposition/ion implantation → metallization → EDS → packaging
Wafer manufacturing → oxidation → etch → photo → deposition/ion implantation → metallization → EDS → packaging
Wafer manufacturing → oxidation → photo → etch → deposition/ion implantation → metallization → EDS → packaging
Wafer manufacturing → oxidation → photo → etch → deposition/ion implantation → metallization → packaging → EDS
explanation:
Answer explanation
After growing an oxide, photolithography prints the template, etching carves it, deposition and ion implantation fill in material or change properties, and metallization wires everything together. Then the chips are tested by EDS while still on the wafer, and finally cut and packaged.

Why the others are wrong
· Option 1: Photolithography prints the template after the film to be etched exists. Doing it before oxidation leaves nothing to pattern.
· Option 2: Etching needs the resist template from photolithography to know where to carve, so it comes after photo.
· Option 4: EDS tests chips before the wafer is cut, so it comes before packaging — the order avoids spending packaging costs on bad chips.

💡 Key point: The order is wafer manufacturing, oxidation, photo, etch, deposition/ion implantation, metallization, EDS, packaging.

question: What is the best reason etching comes after photolithography?
options: The resist template made by photolithography decides where to carve and where to protect
Etching supplies the heat needed to coat the photoresist
Etching must flatten the wafer surface before exposure is possible
Etching can only be done after ion implantation is finished
explanation:
Answer explanation
Etching carves only the areas the template doesn't cover. Where to carve and where to protect is decided by the template photolithography prints in the resist, so photolithography must be done first.

Why the others are wrong
· Option 2: Etching removes film; it doesn't supply heat for resist coating.
· Option 3: Flattening the surface is the job of polishing (CMP); etching doesn't come after photo because of planarization.
· Option 4: Etching and ion implantation don't have a fixed order relative to each other, and this has nothing to do with why etching follows photo.

💡 Key point: The output of one step is the input to the next, so etching follows photolithography.

question: If each step has a 99% good rate and the steps are independent, what is closest to the overall yield of a wafer after 100 steps?
options: About 99%
About 90%
About 63%
About 37%
explanation:
Answer explanation
Overall yield is the product of each step's good rate, so it's $0.99^{100}$, about 0.37. Losing just 1% per step wipes out more than half the total once 100 steps pile up.

Why the others are wrong
· Option 1: This treats the overall yield as equal to one step's rate. Yield multiplies step rates, so it drops as steps accumulate.
· Option 2: This would be the result after 100 steps at a 99.9% good rate per step.
· Option 3: This mistakes the probability of at least one failure (1 minus 0.37) for the yield.

💡 Key point: Yield is the product of step-by-step good rates; 99% over 100 steps gives about 37%.

question: What happens when a voltage at or above the threshold voltage is applied to an NMOS gate?
options: The gate insulator melts and a large current flows into the gate
A channel forms at the surface under the gate, and current flows between source and drain
The channel between source and drain disappears, cutting off current
The p-type substrate turns n-type and the whole device becomes a conductor
explanation:
Answer explanation
The threshold voltage is the minimum gate voltage at which a channel starts to form. At or above it, electrons gather at the surface under the gate to form a channel, connecting source and drain so current flows.

Why the others are wrong
· Option 1: The gate is separated from the substrate by an insulator, so almost no current flows into it.
· Option 3: The channel disappears when the gate voltage drops below the threshold.
· Option 4: Electrons gather only at the surface under the gate to form the channel; the doping type of the whole substrate doesn't change.

💡 Key point: When the gate voltage exceeds the threshold voltage, a channel forms and connects source and drain.

question: What is the best reason a CMOS inverter uses little power while its input stays constant?
options: One of the two is off, blocking the path from supply to ground
Both transistors are off, so the output connects to neither side
Both transistors are on, so current drains out all at once
The gate insulator gets thicker, so leakage disappears
explanation:
Answer explanation
When the input is 0, only the PMOS is on; when it's 1, only the NMOS is on. The one that's on connects the output to the supply or ground, and the one that's off blocks the path from supply to ground, so almost no current flows.

Why the others are wrong
· Option 2: With the input set, one side is always on, so the output is connected to the supply or ground.
· Option 3: If both were on together, current would flow from supply to ground, increasing power.
· Option 4: Low power comes from the structure that blocks the supply-to-ground path, not from insulator thickness.

💡 Key point: CMOS draws current mainly when values switch; while holding, one side blocks the path.

question: Which memory is suited to storing data, like photo files, that must remain when power is off?
options: DRAM, which holds charge in a capacitor and needs refresh
SRAM, which holds values with cross-coupled inverters
A diode made from a single PN junction
NAND flash, which traps electrons inside the gate
explanation:
Answer explanation
NAND flash traps electrons inside a gate surrounded by insulator, shifting the threshold voltage, and the value remains as long as the electrons stay trapped. So data persists even when power is off.

Why the others are wrong
· Option 1: DRAM is volatile memory whose charge slowly leaks and whose values vanish when power is off.
· Option 2: SRAM is also volatile, needing power to hold values; it's mainly used for caches.
· Option 3: A diode passes current in one direction and doesn't store information.

💡 Key point: Non-volatile memory that survives power-off is NAND flash; DRAM and SRAM are volatile.

question: What changed in the move from FinFET to GAA nanosheets?
options: The number of channel sides wrapped by the gate went from three to four
The structure got simpler, with the gate wrapping only the top side of the channel
Power lines moved to the back of the wafer, lightening front-side wiring
N-type and p-type transistors were stacked on top of each other to save area
explanation:
Answer explanation
In a FinFET, the gate wraps the top and both sides of the fin-shaped channel. GAA nanosheets turn the channel into horizontal sheets wrapped on all four sides, increasing control and reducing leakage.

Why the others are wrong
· Option 2: Wrapping just one side is the planar structure that came before FinFET.
· Option 3: Moving power lines to the back is backside power, a separate branch from transistor structure changes.
· Option 4: Stacking n-type and p-type vertically is CFET, the candidate after GAA.

💡 Key point: Planar 1 side, FinFET 3 sides, GAA 4 sides — the gate wraps more and more.

question: What is the best reason backside power reduces front-side wiring congestion?
options: It removes all signal lines and leaves only power lines
It changes the wiring metal from copper to silicon
It moves power lines to the back so the front carries only signal lines
It shortens the exposure wavelength to make wires thinner
explanation:
Answer explanation
Traditionally, power and signal lines shared the same front-side wiring layers. Moving power lines to the back frees up front-side wiring, and shorter power connections also reduce voltage drop.

Why the others are wrong
· Option 1: Signal lines are still needed and stay on the front.
· Option 2: Backside power changes where power lines go, not the wiring material.
· Option 4: Shortening the wavelength is a direction for lithography and has nothing to do with backside power.

💡 Key point: Backside power sends power lines to the back, reducing front-side congestion and voltage drop.

question: What is an advantage of attaching small chiplets to an interposer instead of making one large chip?
options: No connections between chips are needed, so signals get faster and design gets easier
Splitting into small pieces reduces defect losses, and each chip can use its own process
All chips must be made on the same process, which simplifies design
Chips get larger, increasing the number of good parts per wafer
explanation:
Answer explanation
The smaller a chip, the less area is thrown away when a defect lands on it, so yield loss drops. Also, only the chips that need it, like compute chips, can be made on expensive cutting-edge processes, while the rest use mature processes.

Why the others are wrong
· Option 1: Chiplets actually add chip-to-chip connections, so connection design becomes more important.
· Option 3: An advantage of chiplets is that each function can use a different process.
· Option 4: Larger chips raise the risk of defects and lower yield, so splitting them up is the better approach.

💡 Key point: Chiplets split designs into small pieces to raise yield and let each chip use its own process.
